passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Declined Insurance Claim

emails.subject: Claim 77-3391 — declined for non-disclosure
emails.body:
Dear Claims,

My escape-of-water claim has been declined on the ground that I did not disclose that the property had been underpinned in 1998.

I accept that I did not disclose it. I did not know it. I bought the house in 2016 and the underpinning is not mentioned in the survey I received, the sale documents I signed, or anything I was ever shown. Your letter says I "failed to disclose a material fact". I would not describe finding out about my own house from a claims decision as a failure to disclose it.

My question is about the question you asked. Your application form asks whether the property "has been subject to structural movement or underpinning". It does not ask whether I am aware of any. Those are different questions, and only one of them is answerable by a person rather than by a building.

So I would like to know: does your policy hold applicants responsible for facts about a property that are not disclosed to them at purchase and not discoverable from the documents they receive? If it does, I would like that confirmed in writing, because it is not what a reasonable applicant would understand the form to mean. If it does not, then the decline is wrong.

I am not asking you to pay a claim you do not owe. I am asking which of those two positions you hold.

Sincerely,
Bronagh Kilbride

emails.subject: RE: Claim 77-3391 — declined for non-disclosure
emails.body:
Dear Ms Kilbride,

We hold the second position, and the decline was wrong. It has been overturned and your claim is being assessed on its merits. You should hear within ten working days.

You have also identified a genuine defect in our wording, and I would rather say so than treat this as a one-off. Our duty-of-disclosure test is whether an applicant knew or ought reasonably to have known a fact. The application form does not reflect that test; it asks a question about the building. A form that asks a question the policy does not ask is a form that will keep producing this outcome, and the assessor who declined your claim applied the form correctly.

The wording has gone to our compliance team with a recommendation to change it to "to the best of your knowledge, has the property been...". I am not going to tell you it will be changed, because that is not my decision, and I have seen recommendations sit for a year.

Two things I should add without being asked.

We have declined four other claims on this ground in the past two years. I am having all four reviewed against the knew-or-ought-to-have-known test rather than against the form. I do not yet know what that review will find.

And you should be aware that an overturned decline can still appear on industry databases if it was recorded before reversal. I have requested that the record be amended. If a future insurer raises it with you, ask them to check the amendment and quote this claim number.

Regards,
Severin Adeyemi
Claims Review Manager

passages.title: Why People Do Not Switch, Claim or Complain
passages.content:
Financial markets are designed on the assumption that consumers respond to price and to poor treatment by moving elsewhere. Most do not, and the reasons are better documented than the assumption is.

Switching rates for current accounts, insurance and energy are consistently low even where the saving is substantial and the process takes minutes. The dominant explanation is not laziness but expected effort: consumers reliably overestimate how long switching takes and how likely something is to go wrong, and that estimate is formed from the worst experience they have heard about rather than the average. Providers benefit from this asymmetry without doing anything, and the customers who stay longest are frequently charged most — the loyalty penalty, which is not a penalty for loyalty so much as a price for inertia.

Claiming behaviour follows a similar pattern with an additional element. Studies of eligible non-claimants find that the strongest predictor is not awareness of the benefit but expectation of the process: people who believe a claim will be difficult, intrusive or humiliating do not begin one, and prior contact with a system that behaved that way is the best predictor of all. This means service quality has a demand effect. A process experienced as degrading reduces uptake of the next thing the same body offers, whether or not it is related.

Complaint data carry a bias that is rarely acknowledged when they are used to measure performance. Complaints correlate with confidence, time and language proficiency more than with the severity of the problem. An organisation reading its complaint volume as a measure of harm is reading a measure of who felt able to speak, and the groups least likely to complain are often those with most cause.

There is also a well-documented gap between stated and actual behaviour. Surveys asking whether people would switch after poor service produce high figures; observed switching after the same events is far lower. This is not dishonesty. It reflects the difference between judging a situation and acting in one, and it means research that asks intentions overstates the discipline the market exerts.

The implication is that consumer protection built on the assumption of an active, mobile customer will under-protect the people it most needs to reach, because it is designed around a behaviour that the evidence says is uncommon.

passages.title: Should Banks Be Required to Keep Branches Open?

viewpoints.name: Regulator Astrid Lindqvist
viewpoints.text: We imposed a closure moratorium on last-branch-in-town cases and I would describe the result carefully. Access was preserved and usage did not recover — the branches stayed open and stayed quiet, which critics read as proof the policy failed. I read it differently: the people still using them are disproportionately older, disabled or running small cash businesses, and a facility used by few can still be the only route for those few. What I would not claim is that we reversed the decline in branch banking. We did not, and we were never going to.

viewpoints.name: Piotr Wesolowski, bank operations director
viewpoints.text: Branch economics are genuinely poor and I will not pretend otherwise, but the honest objection to a mandate is narrower than the one we usually make publicly. It is that a requirement to keep a building open does not require it to be staffed by anyone who can do anything. Comply cheaply and you get a branch with reduced hours, one member of staff and no lending authority, which satisfies the rule and helps nobody. Regulate the service, not the premises, or you will get premises.

viewpoints.name: Dr Cheng Wei-Lin, financial inclusion researcher
viewpoints.text: The evidence on closures is strong on one point and weak on the one most cited. Closures measurably reduce small-business lending in the affected area, and that finding replicates. The claim that closures directly cause financial exclusion among individuals is weaker, because most affected customers do substitute — into online banking, into another provider, or into cash arrangements with relatives. Substitution is not the same as being fine, and I want the argument made on the lending evidence, which is solid, rather than on the exclusion claim, which is contested.

viewpoints.name: Fionnuala Brennan, post office operator
viewpoints.text: Everyone's solution is that the post office absorbs branch banking, and I am the post office. I was not consulted, my counter fee for a bank transaction is set by an agreement I did not negotiate, and my queue now contains people needing twenty minutes of help with a bank problem I am not trained or paid to solve. I am not refusing the work. I am saying that transferring a service to a smaller business without transferring the funding is not a policy — it is a cost being moved somewhere quieter.
